summary:
İzmir stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward LGBT people has hardened from residual prejudice into documented state policy. Kaos GL's report "A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy" records 313 violations of the right to liberty during 2025, about two and a half times the 2024 figure, together with 299 detention decisions of which 256 were recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record. The same report counts 89 torture or ill-treatment violations and six violations of the right to life, three of them registered as hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected. For the first time in many years an LGBTI+ association was closed, and criminal cases were opened against 11 of its members for human rights advocacy.

A leaked draft of Türkiye's omnibus 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the penal code to punish conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, and its promotion, with up to three years' imprisonment. Participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies would carry up to four years. An amendment to civil code article 40 would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing interventions deemed illegal would face fines and up to seven years in prison, trans people receiving such care up to three years, and courts could order pretrial detention. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warned it would push treatment into unregulated underground settings.

The Erdoğan government frames its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma. The draft had not been passed when reported, but authorities have applied its prohibitions regardless. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in that reporting argue the checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained said police imposed no fines but documented them anyway, and that the new law had not been passed even as enforcement was already being applied.

Foreign visitors stopped at such checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, creating a direct outing risk where appearance does not match the passport gender marker. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Every document check is therefore an occasion on which presentation can be compared against recorded sex.

On 31 July 2025, trans women in a large-city entertainment district were subjected to mass identity-document roundups. Their names were recorded and videos taken, with no official reason given, a pattern that points to profiling rather than law enforcement.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected. In August 2024 a trans woman was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest. Activists treat that reversal as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring by the Truth Justice Memory Center of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

Trans prisoners are held according to registered sex in gendered facilities. A prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, İzmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın coordinated demands for an independent investigation. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees rest on segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. A Prison Insider country profile prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association, using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. No policy or staff training exists to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary basis, transfers disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need for Liberation, based on more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

The enforcement pattern documented in Istanbul runs ahead of legislation: detention practice based on prohibitions that had not been enacted, which indicates that visitors are exposed to administrative and police action regardless of the drafting status of the 11th Judicial Package.

Legal argument in the reporting rests on external standards, specifically Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights, rather than on domestic remedies. The Istanbul mechanism of GBT checks and the 31 July 2025 document roundups show a repeatable tactic that a visitor to any major Turkish city, İzmir included, could encounter.

Documentation of Pride-related violations has continued since 2015 through independent monitoring bodies, and international prison-monitoring data assembled with ILGA World is now part of the evidentiary record on Turkish detention conditions.

Health records now matter to residents directly: hospitals may not record the "other" option on medical-board reports and must issue e-reports, which places transition-related care into searchable official documentation.

Domestic violence against trans people carries an asymmetric state response, illustrated by the August 2024 Bakırköy case in which the attacker was released and the trans victim was referred for arrest.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted is unresolved here: the inventory reports it as a leaked draft pending before the government as of 29 October 2025, and no later legislative record is sourced.

İzmir-specific policing, Pride bans or local detention figures are not sourced in this inventory. The identity-check reporting concerns Istanbul, so it is presented as an illustration of national practice rather than an İzmir finding.

No sourced entry, visa or border-screening rule specific to trans visitors appears in the inventory; the document-carrying obligation and its fine are the only entry-adjacent provisions available.

Passport gender-marker change procedure for Turkish and foreign documents is not covered by these sources and remains unresolved for this record.

The claimed "LGBT opening" framing contested around the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation is described in the source without a named originating authority, so its provenance is unresolved.
